The Half-Life of a Market Edge

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code

Post-publication decay in 189 published equity anomalies, 1926 to 2024

Author

Mehmet Tuğsuz

Published

October 5, 2026

Abstract

Several hundred cross-sectional return predictors have been published since the 1980s. We measure what happens to them after publication, using the 189 usable signals in the Chen and Zimmermann universe through December 2024. Mean monthly long-short returns fall 45 percent from the original sample window to the post-publication window, and the median signal loses 53 percent. The increment attributable to publication itself, over and above the decline that had already set in when the original sample ended, is not statistically significant, so the design does not separate arbitrage from selection in this universe. We rebuild two of the input series from security-level CRSP data to check the dataset. A real-time forecasting exercise over 1995 to 2024 finds that next month’s return on a published signal is weakly predictable, that no model beats another by a margin a test can distinguish, and that the predictive content sits in the signal’s own return history: the publication clock adds nothing once that history is known. At the stock level, with 153 published characteristics as features, a model given only the characteristics that were public in each test year trails the usual model given all of them in every row set and every portfolio, by a few tenths of a point of out-of-sample R-squared; for the linear models the gap in net Sharpe ratio, about a third of a unit, survives a Ledoit-Wolf test in every book. That gap is the look-ahead in the usual setup. In event time around publication, a model refit each year does not lean less on a characteristic after its paper appears; the one estimate that clears conventional significance comes with a pre-trend and is reported as a first pass.

Code: github.com/tugsuz/alpha-decay. A PDF of this page is at alpha-decay.pdf. Every number in the text is computed when the document is rendered, from the two public Chen and Zimmermann files or from result files written by the scripts in the repository.

def ym(mi):
    """Invert mi = year*12 + month. divmod on mi - 1 keeps December in its own year."""
    y, m = divmod(int(mi) - 1, 12)
    return y, m + 1

def mi_to_ts(idx):
    return pd.to_datetime([f"{y}-{m:02d}-01" for y, m in map(ym, idx)])

1 Introduction

A cross-sectional return predictor is a rule: sort stocks on a characteristic, buy one end of the sort and sell the other. Several hundred such rules have been published since Banz (1981). This paper asks what happens to one after the paper that documents it appears.

The question matters to anyone who allocates capital to a published signal. The value of a strategy is the return it will earn from now on, net of costs, times the capital it can carry. Publication changes that return. The recipe becomes common knowledge, capital arrives, and the edge shrinks until what is left no longer pays for the trading it takes to collect it (Grossman and Stiglitz 1980; Shleifer and Vishny 1997). How much the edge shrinks, how fast, and whether it stops at zero or at a floor are the three numbers an allocator needs before deciding how much to put on a strategy and how long to keep it. We measure the first across the whole published universe and take a step toward the second.

The word “decay” has two meanings and we use only one of them. On a trading desk, alpha decay is the speed at which a signal’s forecast loses power after it is computed. It is measured in hours or days and it is an input to how aggressively the signal is traded (Gârleanu and Pedersen 2013). The decay in this paper runs on a slower clock. It is the decline in a strategy’s average monthly return over the years after the strategy becomes public. The two share a mechanism. A short-horizon signal loses its edge within a day because other traders act on the same information quickly; a published monthly signal loses its edge over years because capital takes years to arrive. Below, decay always means the second.

The same logic applies to signals found by machine learning. A model fitted to past returns is a published signal in everything but the journal. Once enough capital trades the same features through similar models, the return the model predicts is competed away in the same way. Published anomalies have one advantage as a laboratory: the date on which each became common knowledge is known, so the decay can be measured against it.

What is known. McLean and Pontiff (2016) find, on 97 anomalies, that long-short returns are 26 percent lower after the original sample ends and 58 percent lower after publication, and they read the gap between those two numbers as the effect of publication itself. Chen and Velikov (2023) add trading costs and find that the average published anomaly earns about four basis points a month net after 2000. Jacobs and Müller (2020) find a reliable post-publication decline only in the United States. Falck, Rej, and Thesmar (2022) find that the year of publication alone explains a large share of how much a strategy’s Sharpe ratio falls out of sample.

What this paper does. We re-measure post-publication decay on the Chen and Zimmermann (2022) universe, which covers 212 predictors through December 2024, about twice the McLean and Pontiff sample and a decade more data. Mean long-short returns fall 45 percent from the original sample window to the post-publication window, and the median signal loses 53 percent. We then test the restriction that separates the two explanations of the decline, arbitrage after publication and selection in the original sample, and we fail to reject it: the three-window design does not identify the channel in this universe. We rebuild two of the input series from security-level CRSP data as a check on the dataset everything else rests on.

Finally we ask whether a forecaster standing in real time, knowing only the signals that had been published by then, could have picked the ones that would keep paying. The answer is modest. A linear regression and gradient boosted trees each earn an out-of-sample R² below one percent, no model beats another by a margin a test can distinguish, and almost all of the predictive content sits in the signal’s own return history. Holding every published signal with equal weight earns a higher Sharpe ratio than any model-based selection. We then move the same question to individual stocks, with 153 published characteristics as features, and fit every model twice: once on the characteristics that were public in each test year and once on all of them. The second set, which is the usual one and contains look-ahead, is ahead of the first in every model, every row set and every portfolio, by a few tenths of a point of out-of-sample R², and for the linear models the gap in net Sharpe ratio, about a third of a unit, survives a Ledoit-Wolf test in every book. In event time around each characteristic’s publication the model does not lean less on it afterwards; the one estimate that clears conventional significance, for the linear model, comes with a pre-trend, so it is reported as a first pass.

Section 2 describes the data, Section 3 the design and the estimator, Section 4 the results and the restriction test, Section 5 the CRSP rebuild, Section 6 the forecasting exercise on the anomaly panel and Section 7 the stock-level one. Section 8 sets out what the design cannot do and what comes next.

2 Data

2.1 The anomaly universe

Chen and Zimmermann (2022) reimplement several hundred published predictors from the original papers and publish the resulting long-short portfolio return series with a documentation file that records, for each signal, the authors, the journal, the publication year, the original sample window and the implementation parameters. We use two files, both free:

File What it holds
PredictorLSretWide.csv monthly long-short returns, one column per signal
SignalDoc.csv one row per signal: acronym, journal, Year, SampleStartYear, SampleEndYear, plus Sign, Stock Weight, LS Quantile, Portfolio Period

The release is October 2025, version 2.0.0. Most series run through December 2024; the option-implied-volatility predictors end in December 2022. This is the first release produced by the authors’ Python translation of their original Stata code, and ChNAnalyst, PriceDelayTstat and Recomm_ShortInterest carry revisions from bug fixes in that translation. All three are in the universe below.

load the two Chen and Zimmermann files

rets = pd.read_csv(DATA / "PredictorLSretWide.csv")

rets["date"] = pd.to_datetime(rets["date"])
doc = pd.read_csv(DATA / "SignalDoc.csv")

2.2 Which signals enter

Three filters, each of which changes the answer.

  1. Predictors only. The authors label some series as placebos, characteristics their own replication finds do not predict returns. Averaging those in would pull every window toward zero and flatter the decay.
  2. The paper’s sample must end strictly before the paper appears. Otherwise the middle window below is empty and the design collapses to two periods.
  3. At least 24 monthly observations in every window, so that a signal cannot enter the post-publication average on the strength of three months.

The third filter keeps the composition fixed. The same signals appear in all three windows, so the decline cannot come from the sample changing between them.

code 
MIN_MONTHS = 24

d = doc[doc["Cat.Signal"] == "Predictor"].dropna(subset=["Year", "SampleEndYear"])
d = d[d["SampleEndYear"] < d["Year"]]                       # filter 2

usable = [c for c in rets.columns if c != "date" and c in set(d["Acronym"])]
long = (rets[["date"] + usable]
        .melt(id_vars="date", var_name="signal", value_name="ret")
        .dropna(subset=["ret"]))

meta = d.set_index("Acronym")[["Year", "SampleEndYear"]]
long["pub_year"] = long["signal"].map(meta["Year"]).astype(int)
long["samp_end"] = long["signal"].map(meta["SampleEndYear"]).astype(int)
long["year"] = long["date"].dt.year

long["window"] = np.select(
    [long["year"] <= long["samp_end"],
     (long["year"] > long["samp_end"]) & (long["year"] < long["pub_year"])],
    ["1_in_sample", "2_post_sample"],
    default="3_post_pub",
)
code 
g = long.groupby(["signal", "window"])["ret"].agg(["mean", "size"]).unstack("window")
complete = (g["size"].fillna(0) >= MIN_MONTHS).all(axis=1)      # filter 3
table = g["mean"][complete].dropna()
table.columns = [c.split("_", 1)[1] for c in table.columns]

N_MATCHED = len(table)
N_PANEL   = long["signal"].nunique()
N_OBS     = len(long)
N_DATES   = long["date"].nunique()

The regression panel holds 212 signals and 173,302 signal-months from 1926-01 to 2024-12, across 1,188 distinct months. The matched table holds the 189 signals that clear all three filters.

3 Design and estimator

3.1 Three windows

We cut each signal’s history at two dates taken from its own paper.

Window Definition What it is
1. in-sample year ≤ SampleEndYear the edge as originally reported
2. post-sample SampleEndYear < year < Year discovered, not yet public
3. post-publication year ≥ Year public, and traded on

Window 2 carries the design. If decay comes from arbitrage, nothing happens until the paper appears: window 2 should look like window 1 and only window 3 falls. If decay comes from selection in the original sample, window 2 is already lower, because stepping outside the author’s chosen sample is enough.

For signal \(i\) let \(\mu_i^{(w)}\) be its mean long-short return in window \(w\). The two estimands are

\[ \delta_1 \;=\; \mathbb{E}_i\!\left[\mu_i^{(2)} - \mu_i^{(1)}\right], \qquad \delta_2 \;=\; \mathbb{E}_i\!\left[\mu_i^{(3)} - \mu_i^{(1)}\right] , \]

and the quantity the two stories disagree about is the increment \(\delta_2 - \delta_1\), the part of the fall that arrives with publication. Arbitrage predicts \(\delta_1 \approx 0\) and \(\delta_2 - \delta_1 < 0\). Pure selection predicts \(\delta_1 < 0\) and \(\delta_2 - \delta_1 \approx 0\).

The estimands are causal effects of publication only if the publication date is as good as random with respect to a signal’s own return path. That is not obviously true. Authors submit when a result looks good, and journals publish with a lag that is itself related to how strong the result is. We read the design as an event study with a pre-period. Section 8 discusses what would tighten it.

3.2 The regression

\[ r_{it} \;=\; \alpha_i \;+\; \beta_1 D^{\mathrm{post\text{-}sample}}_{it} \;+\; \beta_2 D^{\mathrm{post\text{-}pub}}_{it} \;+\; \varepsilon_{it} \tag{1}\]

where \(r_{it}\) is signal \(i\)’s long-short return in month \(t\) in percent per month, the two \(D\) variables are the window indicators, and window 1 is the omitted category, so \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) are read against the in-sample mean. The signal fixed effect \(\alpha_i\) makes this a within comparison. Without it, \(\beta_2\) would partly reflect the fact that signals published long ago are different signals from those published recently.

We absorb the fixed effects by subtracting each signal’s own mean from every variable,

\[ \tilde z_{it} \;=\; z_{it} - \bar z_i , \qquad \bar z_i = \frac{1}{T_i}\sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}_i} z_{it} . \]

By the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem (Frisch and Waugh 1933; Lovell 1963) a regression of \(\tilde r\) on \(\tilde D\) returns the same \(\hat\beta\) as the regression with 212 signal dummies. The coefficients are identified from variation over time within a signal.

3.3 Clustering by date

Two long-short portfolios in the same month are not independent draws. They are built from the same stocks in the same market, and a month in which value and momentum both do badly moves many of them together. We cluster by date, which allows arbitrary correlation within a month. Clustering by signal would allow arbitrary correlation within a signal over time, which is the wrong axis here (Petersen 2009). With 1,188 months the cluster count is large enough for the asymptotics to be reliable.

Let \(g = 1,\dots,G\) index months, \(\tilde X_g\) the rows of the demeaned design matrix in month \(g\) and \(\hat u_g\) the residuals there. The covariance estimator is

\[ \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta) \;=\; c \,\bigl(\tilde X'\tilde X\bigr)^{-1} \Bigl[\textstyle\sum_{g=1}^{G} \bigl(\tilde X_g' \hat u_g\bigr)\bigl(\tilde X_g' \hat u_g\bigr)'\Bigr] \bigl(\tilde X'\tilde X\bigr)^{-1}, \qquad c \;=\; \frac{G}{G-1}\cdot\frac{n-1}{n-k} . \tag{2}\]

Scores are summed inside a month before they are squared, so correlation within the month is absorbed. The finite-sample factor \(c\) is the usual one; it does not subtract the absorbed fixed effects from the degrees of freedom, and with 173,302 observations that changes the standard errors by about 0.1 percent.

code 
def within(df, cols, by):
    """Demean `cols` within groups of `by`. Identical to including group dummies."""
    return df[cols] - df.groupby(by)[cols].transform("mean")

def cluster_ols(y, X, cluster):
    """OLS with a cluster-robust covariance matrix, written out."""
    XtX_inv = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
    beta    = XtX_inv @ (X.T @ y)
    u       = X * (y - X @ beta)[:, None]

    codes = pd.factorize(cluster)[0]
    G     = codes.max() + 1
    meat  = np.zeros((X.shape[1], X.shape[1]))
    for g in range(G):                       # sum scores inside a cluster, then square
        s = u[codes == g].sum(axis=0)
        meat += np.outer(s, s)

    n, k = X.shape
    c    = (G / (G - 1)) * ((n - 1) / (n - k))
    V    = c * (XtX_inv @ meat @ XtX_inv)
    return beta, V, G

def fit(sub):
    s = sub.copy()
    s["post_sample"] = (s["window"] == "2_post_sample").astype(float)
    s["post_pub"]    = (s["window"] == "3_post_pub").astype(float)
    dm = within(s, ["ret", "post_sample", "post_pub"], "signal")
    y  = dm["ret"].to_numpy()
    X  = dm[["post_sample", "post_pub"]].to_numpy()
    return cluster_ols(y, X, s["date"].to_numpy())

151 of 189 (80 percent) earn less after publication than in sample, and 32 (17 percent) have a negative mean long-short return once public. 109 were already lower in window 2.

4.2 The panel regression

McLean and Pontiff (2016) report about 26 percent post-sample and 58 percent post-publication over 97 anomalies. This universe is about twice as large and includes weaker and less replicated signals. That is the first explanation for the smaller numbers and it can be tested by re-running the design on their 97.

4.3 What the estimates do not show

Read Table 2 quickly and a conclusion suggests itself: \(\beta_2\) is sharply estimated and \(\beta_1\) is not, so publication is what kills the edge. That conclusion does not survive a test.

“Publication matters over and above the end of the sample” is the restriction \(H_0: \beta_2 = \beta_1\), that is \(R\beta = 0\) with \(R = (-1,\;1)\). The standard error of \(R\hat\beta\) comes from the same clustered covariance matrix, and it is not the sum of the two individual standard errors, because \(\hat\beta_1\) and \(\hat\beta_2\) covary:

\[ \mathrm{se}\!\left(\hat\beta_2 - \hat\beta_1\right) = \sqrt{R \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta) R'} = \sqrt{\widehat V_{11} + \widehat V_{22} - 2\widehat V_{12}} . \tag{3}\]

Comparing two \(t\)-statistics, one significant and one not, does not test whether the coefficients differ. Equation 3 does.

code 
R = np.array([-1.0, 1.0])

def restriction(beta, V):
    diff = R @ beta
    se   = np.sqrt(R @ V @ R)
    return diff, se, diff / se

diff_f, sed_f, td_f = restriction(beta_f, V_f)
diff_m, sed_m, td_m = restriction(beta_m, V_m)
corr_f = V_f[0, 1] / np.sqrt(V_f[0, 0] * V_f[1, 1])

The incremental effect of publication, over and above the decline that had already happened by the time the original sample ended, is not significant at the 5 percent level (|t| = 1.67 against a critical value of 1.96). The estimated correlation between \(\hat\beta_1\) and \(\hat\beta_2\) is 0.33, so the difference is less precisely estimated than \(\hat\beta_2\) alone.

The point estimates are consistent with publication being the operative channel. The data do not support that reading at conventional levels, and the three-window design does not separate the arbitrage channel from the selection channel in this universe. What the data do support: the post-publication decline is precisely estimated, the post-sample decline is not, and the difference between them is too imprecise to claim.

A second limitation concerns calendar time. Publication years in this universe cluster between the early 1990s and the mid-2010s, so for most signals “after publication” also means “after about 2001”. Chordia, Subrahmanyam, and Tong (2014) document a decline in anomaly returns across the board after decimalization, with growth in hedge fund assets, short interest and turnover as the drivers. A specification with calendar-time fixed effects would separate the two, and with staggered publication dates it is identified from the timing differences across signals. We have not run it here; it is the first item in Section 8.

5 Rebuilding two signals from CRSP

Everything above is computed from return series that somebody else constructed. We therefore rebuild two signals from security-level CRSP data and score them month by month against the published versions: Size, about the simplest anomaly there is, and Mom12m, which has a formation window, a skip month and overlapping holding periods and is easy to get subtly wrong.

The pull (03_crsp_pull.py) and the rebuild (04_build_anomalies.py) need a WRDS subscription. This section reads the committed result files and needs nothing.

5.1 Portfolio construction

At each formation month \(m\) the cross-section is sorted on the signal and cut into \(n = 1/q\) buckets, where \(q\) comes from SignalDoc: \(q = 0.5\) for Size, because Banz (1981) splits the market in two, and \(q = 0.1\) for Mom12m. For a bucket \(B_m\) and a horizon \(h\),

\[ \bar r^{\,B}_{m,h} \;=\; \frac{\sum_{i \in B_m} w_{i,m}\, r_{i,\,m+h}}{\sum_{i \in B_m} w_{i,m}} , \qquad \mathrm{LS}^{(h)}_{m} \;=\; s \cdot \Bigl( \bar r^{\,\mathrm{top}}_{m,h} - \bar r^{\,\mathrm{bot}}_{m,h} \Bigr), \]

with \(w_{i,m} = 1\) for equal weighting and \(w_{i,m} = \mathrm{mthcap}_{i,m}\) for value weighting, and \(s = \pm 1\) the sign from SignalDoc. For Size the sign is \(-1\): the anomaly is small minus big, and reversing it produces a significant result with the wrong label.

Portfolio Period is a holding period with overlapping cohorts (Jegadeesh and Titman 1993). The return booked in calendar month \(c\) averages the cohorts formed at \(c-1, \dots, c-H\),

\[ \mathrm{LS}_{c} \;=\; \frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H} \mathrm{LS}^{(h)}_{\,c-h} . \tag{4}\]

The momentum signal is the twelve-month return ending one month before formation,

\[ s^{\mathrm{mom}}_{i,m} \;=\; \exp\!\Biggl(\;\sum_{\tau = m-k-11}^{\,m-k} \log\bigl(1 + r_{i\tau}\bigr)\Biggr) - 1, \qquad k = 1 , \tag{5}\]

defined only where the stock has a contiguous monthly record across the window. Size is \(s^{\mathrm{size}}_{i,m} = \log(\mathrm{mthcap}_{i,m})\).

5.2 The comparison

read the committed rebuild results 
def load_rebuild(name, col):
    df = pd.read_csv(OUT / f"rebuild_{name}.csv")
    o  = df.dropna(subset=[col, "theirs"]).copy()
    o["gap"] = o[col] - o["theirs"]
    o["year"] = [ym(v)[0] for v in o["mi"]]
    return o

reb = {"Size": load_rebuild("Size", "mine"),
       "Mom12m": load_rebuild("Mom12m", "mine_hold1")}
COL = {"Size": "mine", "Mom12m": "mine_hold1"}

def gap_t(o):
    g = o["gap"].to_numpy()
    return g.mean(), g.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(g))

def corr(o, name):
    return float(np.corrcoef(o[COL[name]], o["theirs"])[0, 1])
code 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.6, 3.4))
for ax, name in zip(axes, ["Size", "Mom12m"]):
    o = reb[name]; x = mi_to_ts(o["mi"])
    a = (1 + o[COL[name]] / 100).cumprod().to_numpy()
    b = (1 + o["theirs"] / 100).cumprod().to_numpy()
    ax.plot(x, b, color=ORANGE, lw=1.5, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=2,
            label="Chen and Zimmermann")
    ax.plot(x, a, color=BLUE,   lw=1.1, label="rebuilt from CRSP", zorder=3)
    ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_title(name)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False); ax.margins(x=0.02)
    ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)

axes[0].set_ylabel("cumulative long-short, log scale")
axes[0].annotate("the two lines coincide", xy=(0.50, 0.08), xycoords="axes fraction",
                 fontsize=8.5, color=MUTED)
axes[1].annotate("same turning points,\nshallower slope", xy=(0.52, 0.06),
                 xycoords="axes fraction", fontsize=8.5, color=MUTED)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Size reproduces almost exactly: a difference of +0.002 percent a month over 1,182 months, correlation 0.992. In Figure 3 the two lines are hard to tell apart across a century.

Momentum reproduces in shape and comes in light in level. The right-hand panel shows two lines with the same turning points and different slopes, which on a log scale is a roughly constant per-month shortfall.

5.3 Is the momentum gap real?

code 
o = reb["Mom12m"]
mg, sg = gap_t(o)
sd_gap = o["gap"].std(ddof=1)

# 1. thin pre-1963 data, when CRSP covers NYSE only?
pre, post = o[o["year"] < 1963], o[o["year"] >= 1963]
(mpre, spre), (mpost, spost) = gap_t(pre), gap_t(post)

# 2. a uniform implementation difference, present every month?
share_below = (o["gap"] < 0).mean()

# 3. or a tail?
worst   = o.reindex(o["gap"].abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index)
share60 = worst.head(60)["gap"].sum() / len(o) / mg
cut     = o["gap"].abs().quantile(0.90)
trim_all  = o[o["gap"].abs() <= cut]["gap"].mean()
cut_pre   = pre["gap"].abs().quantile(0.90)
trim_pre  = pre[pre["gap"].abs() <= cut_pre]["gap"].mean()
corr_abs  = float(np.corrcoef(o["gap"].abs(), o["theirs"].abs())[0, 1])

A momentum long-short series is volatile, and so is the month-by-month difference between two implementations of one. The gap has a standard deviation of 2.03 percent a month, so a mean of -0.107 over 1,174 months carries t = -1.82. Before 1963 it is t = -0.74; from 1963 on, t = -1.94. Neither period rejects equality.

We checked three explanations.

First, thin early data. CRSP covers NYSE only until mid-1962, so the natural guess is that the gap sits before 1963 and the modern period replicates cleanly. It does not. The gap is -0.092 before 1963 and -0.116 after.

Second, a uniform implementation difference. If a slightly different screen produced a slightly different portfolio every month, the sign of the difference would be persistent. The rebuilt series is below the published one in 53.0 percent of months, a coin flip.

Third, a tail. The 60 months with the largest absolute gap, 5 percent of the sample, carry 100 percent of the mean difference. Trimming the largest decile of months takes the full-sample gap to -0.051 and flips the pre-1963 gap to +0.068. The absolute gap correlates 0.37 with the absolute size of that month’s published return.

All eight fall between 1931 and 1943, in the momentum crashes and rebounds of the Depression and the war years, when past losers surge and the extreme deciles turn over violently (Daniel and Moskowitz 2016). September 1939 is the rebound at the outbreak of war, and the 1932 and 1933 months are the largest momentum reversals on record. The post-war crash months rank lower: December 2008 is 14th by absolute gap and March 2009 is 17th. In months like these a single imputed price, or one stock that delists inside a holding period, moves a bucket mean by percentage points, and two implementations of a decile sort part company. Shumway (1997) is the classic statement of how much the treatment of disappearing stocks matters.

We tried no screen variants. The remaining 0.107 percent a month could be closed by searching filter combinations until the rebuilt series matched the published one. That would be fitting the replication to its target, and it is the behaviour this paper sets out to measure. One signal reproduces exactly; the other reproduces to within sampling error.

5.4 A definition error that correlation did not catch

SignalDoc defines Mom12m over “months t-12 and t-1”. Month \(t\) is excluded, which is the \(k = 1\) in Equation 5. Our first implementation used \(m-11,\dots,m\), which pulls short-term reversal (Jegadeesh 1990) into a momentum signal. Last month’s return is negatively autocorrelated, so including it adds an effect of the opposite sign.

code 
# `mine` and `mine_noskip` both use the documented three-month holding period. They
# differ in one thing only: whether month t is inside the formation window.
ns = (pd.read_csv(OUT / "rebuild_Mom12m.csv")
        .dropna(subset=["mine", "mine_noskip", "theirs"]))
mean_skip   = ns["mine"].mean()
mean_noskip = ns["mine_noskip"].mean()
mean_theirs = ns["theirs"].mean()
corr_noskip = float(np.corrcoef(ns["mine_noskip"], ns["theirs"])[0, 1])

With everything else fixed at the documented three-month holding period, dropping the skip takes the long-short mean from 0.652 to 0.459 percent a month, against a published 0.899. Rebalanced monthly, where no cohort skips at all, the mean fell to -0.009 percent a month: the premium disappeared.

The correlation with the published series stayed at 0.974 throughout, peaking at lag 0. Correlation confirms that the merge and the calendar are right. It says nothing about whether the signal definition is right, because a signal formed on the wrong window is still mostly the same portfolio. Only the level catches this.

6 Can a model pick the survivors in real time?

The decay in this section is the one measured above: the decline in a published signal’s monthly long-short return over the years after publication. We ask a forecasting question about it. Standing in a given month, knowing only the signals that had been published by then, could a forecaster have picked the ones that would pay next month, and does a flexible model do this better than a linear one?

The question is the allocator’s. A fund that trades published signals has to decide, every month, which of them to keep. It also tests the mechanism from a different angle. If decay is a predictable function of time since publication, a model given that clock should use it. If the information is already in the signal’s own return history, the clock should add nothing once that history is in the model.

6.1 Information set and panel

One row is a signal in a month; the target is that signal’s long-short return next month. A forecaster in month \(t\) knows which signals have been published (publication year strictly before the year of \(t\)), each published signal’s documented sample window and the characteristics of its paper, and each published signal’s return history up to \(t\), including the months before the paper appeared, since a public recipe can be backfilled. The forecaster knows nothing about signals not yet published. A signal therefore enters the panel, for training and for testing, only in the years after its publication year. This is the whole of the no-look-ahead rule, and it removes most of the sample before 1995, when fewer than two dozen signals were public.

read the committed results of 05_ml_panel.py 
r2   = pd.read_csv(OUT / "ml_r2.csv", index_col=0)
dm   = pd.read_csv(OUT / "ml_dm.csv")
port = pd.read_csv(OUT / "ml_portfolio.csv", index_col=0)
port.index = pd.PeriodIndex(port.index, freq="M")
imp  = pd.read_csv(OUT / "ml_importance.csv", index_col=0)
curve = pd.read_csv(OUT / "ml_decay_curve.csv", index_col=0)
tuning = pd.read_csv(OUT / "ml_tuning.csv")

LAB = {"zero": "zero forecast", "own_mean": "own historical mean", "ols": "OLS",
       "enet": "elastic net", "gbrt": "gradient boosted trees",
       "mlp": "neural network (16 units)"}
MODELS = ["zero", "own_mean", "ols", "enet", "gbrt", "mlp"]
N_TEST = int(r2["n_test_rows"].iloc[0])

def perf(x):
    m, s = x.mean(), x.std(ddof=1)
    return m, s, (m / s) * np.sqrt(12), m / (s / np.sqrt(len(x)))

def dm_t(bench, model):
    return float(dm[(dm["benchmark"] == bench) & (dm["model"] == model)]["dm_t"].iloc[0])

Every model sees the same 27 features, all known at \(t\):

  • the signal’s own history: last month’s return, its mean over the past 12, 36 and 60 months and over its whole history, and its 12-month volatility;
  • event time: months since the end of the paper’s sample, months since publication, and the two indicators that follow from them;
  • the paper: publication year, length of the original sample, the \(t\)-statistic and mean return the original paper reported, the quantile cut, the holding period, whether the portfolio is value-weighted, whether the sort is on a discrete variable, the data type of the characteristic and whether the journal is one of the three top finance journals;
  • market state, built from the panel itself: last month’s equal-weighted return across the signals that were public, and its 12-month mean and volatility.

Nothing comes from outside the two input files.

6.2 Models and validation

Two benchmarks fit nothing: a forecast of zero, and the signal’s own historical mean return. Against them we fit a linear regression, an elastic net, gradient boosted trees and a neural network with one hidden layer of 16 units, all in scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011). The design follows Gu, Kelly, and Xiu (2020): an expanding window with one refit per calendar year, test years 1995 to 2024; hyperparameters chosen on the last eight years of each training sample, after which the model is refit on the whole sample; and out-of-sample \(R^2\) measured against a zero forecast. Time is kept by the target month. A test year collects the forecasts whose target month falls in that year, every row used to fit or tune the model for it has a target month before January of that year, and the code checks that boundary at each refit. The out-of-sample \(R^2\) is

\[ R^2_{\mathrm{oos}} \;=\; 1 - \frac{\sum_{i,t}\bigl(r_{i,t+1} - \hat r_{i,t+1}\bigr)^2} {\sum_{i,t} r_{i,t+1}^{2}} . \]

We also report \(R^2\) against the own-mean benchmark, which is the harder test. The tuning grids are small on purpose: nine settings for the elastic net, four for the trees with the number of trees chosen on the validation sample, two for the network with three random restarts averaged. Every setting tried is in output/ml_tuning.csv, 450 rows in all. Forecast accuracy is compared with the Diebold and Mariano (1995) test on the monthly average loss differential across signals, with a Newey and West (1987) variance at twelve lags.

6.3 Results

code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.3))
ms = ["own_mean", "ols", "enet", "gbrt", "mlp"]
names = ["own historical\nmean", "OLS", "elastic net", "gradient\nboosted trees",
         "neural network\n(16 units)"]
vals = [100 * r2.loc[m, "r2_vs_zero"] for m in ms]
ax.bar(names, vals, color=BLUE, width=0.6, zorder=3)
for i, v in enumerate(vals):
    ax.text(i, v + 0.02 if v >= 0 else v - 0.02, f"{v:+.2f}%", ha="center",
            va="bottom" if v >= 0 else "top", fontsize=9, color=INK)
ax.axhline(0, color=INK, lw=0.8)
ax.set_ylabel("out-of-sample R², %")
ax.set_title(f"{N_TEST:,} signal-months, test years 1995 to 2024")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
lo, hi = min(vals + [0]), max(vals + [0])
ax.set_ylim(lo - 0.15, hi + 0.18)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Three things stand out in Table 6.

The numbers are small. The linear regression explains 0.84 percent of next month’s variation, the trees 0.88 percent, and the own-mean benchmark alone 0.62 percent. This is the order of magnitude Gu, Kelly, and Xiu (2020) report for individual stocks at the monthly horizon; monthly long-short returns are mostly noise.

No model beats another by a margin a test can distinguish. Against the own-mean benchmark OLS adds 0.23 percent, the trees 0.26 percent and the network -0.84 percent. The Diebold-Mariano statistic for OLS against the own mean is -0.29, for the trees against OLS +0.42, and for the network against OLS -1.15. The tree number also depends on the tuning path: holding any one of the four grid settings fixed through all thirty refits gives an \(R^2\) between 0.70 and 0.93 percent, so the gap between the trees and the linear model is inside the range the trees cover on their own. (The fit uses no subsampling, so a setting fixes the result; seeds play no role.) On this panel a model that can represent interactions and nonlinearities finds none that a test can see.

Predictability does not fall with age. The \(R^2\) is as high for signals more than ten years past publication as for signals in their first three years. Whatever is predictable about a published signal’s next return is still predictable long after the paper.

Table 7 says where the predictive content sits. Shuffling the signal’s own return history raises the test error by 0.423 for the trees and 0.535 for OLS. The next largest group for the trees is market state, at 0.068; every other group moves the error by less than 0.011 in either direction, and for several of them the error falls, which is what noise looks like under permutation. Event time in particular adds nothing once the signal’s own history is in the model.

6.4 The decay curve, conditional and unconditional

code 
raw = curve.dropna(subset=["mean"])
pdp = curve.dropna(subset=["pd_gbrt"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.8))
ax.errorbar(raw.index / 12, raw["mean"], yerr=1.96 * raw["se"], fmt="o", ms=3.6,
            color=MUTED, capsize=2, lw=0.8, zorder=3, label="mean return in event-time bin")
ax.plot(pdp.index / 12, pdp["pd_gbrt"], color=BLUE, lw=2, zorder=4,
        label="gradient boosted trees, partial dependence")
ax.plot(pdp.index / 12, pdp["pd_ols"], color=ORANGE, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=4,
        label="OLS, partial dependence")
ax.axvline(0, color=INK, lw=0.8)
ax.axhline(0, color=MUTED, lw=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("years since publication")
ax.set_ylabel("long-short return, %/month")
ax.set_title("Return against time since publication")
ax.legend(fontsize=8.2, loc="upper right")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Figure 5 puts the two readings of decay side by side. The dots are unconditional: the average return of published signals in each year after publication, averaged across whatever signals were in the panel. They sit around 0.31 percent a month, close to the post-publication window mean in Table 1, and they show no trend over twenty years. The lines are conditional. They show what each model predicts as the publication clock moves while the signal’s own history and everything else is held fixed. The OLS line falls from 0.47 at publication to 0.41 twenty years later: the monthly return drops by about 0.3 basis points for each year that passes. The tree line is flat at 0.47.

The two readings are consistent. Decay shows up in the level of the dots relative to the in-sample mean in Table 1, which is the result of Section 4. It does not show up as a slope within the post-publication period, and it does not show up as a function of the clock once the model knows the signal’s recent returns. Whatever the publication date tells a forecaster is already in the return series by the time the forecaster could use it.

6.5 Choosing among published signals

code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.8))
for m, color, ls in [("ols", ORANGE, (0, (4, 2))), ("gbrt", BLUE, "-"),
                     ("own_mean", MUTED, (0, (1, 1.5)))]:
    cum = (1 + port[f"{m}_top"] / 100).cumprod()
    ax.plot(cum.index.to_timestamp(), cum, color=color, ls=ls, lw=1.5,
            label=f"top fifth by {LAB[m]}", zorder=3)
cum = (1 + port["all"] / 100).cumprod()
ax.plot(cum.index.to_timestamp(), cum, color=INK, lw=1.3, label="all published signals",
        zorder=4)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_ylabel("value of one dollar, log scale")
ax.set_title("Choosing among published signals")
ax.legend(fontsize=8.2, loc="upper left")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False); ax.margins(x=0.02)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Table 8 is the allocator’s table. Holding every published signal with equal weight earns 0.38 percent a month at a volatility of 1.00, a Sharpe ratio of 1.31. Ranking signals by their own historical mean and holding the top fifth raises the mean to 0.71 and the Sharpe ratio to 1.36. Ranking by the OLS forecast raises the mean further, to 1.03, and doubles the volatility, so the Sharpe ratio falls to 0.94; the trees give 1.00 and 0.89. The models earn their higher mean by selecting volatile signals, and a mean-squared-error forecast of return has no reason to care about volatility. The long-short versions of these portfolios, which also short the bottom fifth, have the same character.

Three cautions. These are portfolios of long-short portfolios and carry no trading costs; Chen and Velikov (2023) show how much of a published anomaly’s gross return the costs take. The return to “the top fifth by own mean” is the return to persistence in the cross-section of published anomalies, which is a statement about the data, not a strategy we would expect to survive its own publication. And the own-mean Sharpe ratio is sensitive to one detail of the universe rule: a signal published in year \(y-1\) first enters in the December feature month of that year, which forecasts January \(y\). Those first-month rows, 189 in all, carry high historical means, are often selected into the top fifth, and earn little; with them the top-fifth Sharpe ratio is 1.36, and under a rule that admits a signal only from the following February it is 1.52.

6.6 What this section does and does not show

It shows that, in real time and without look-ahead, next month’s return on a published signal is weakly predictable, that the predictability is linear and lives in the signal’s own history, and that a model with no access to the publication date would do as well as one with it. It does not show that machine learning cannot find structure in anomaly returns: the features here are coarse, the panel has about 48,000 test rows, and a model given the underlying stock-level data would face a different problem. It also does not touch the horizon a trading desk means by decay, which would need daily or intraday portfolio returns.

7 Stock-level forecasts with and without look-ahead

The panel above has one row per published signal and about 48,000 test rows. The question is usually asked one level down, on individual stocks, with the characteristics as features (Gu, Kelly, and Xiu 2020), and that is where the two things this paper cares about can be measured directly. The first is look-ahead in the choice of features. A model fitted today on every characteristic that has ever been published uses, in 1995, characteristics whose papers appeared in 2010. The gap between that model and one restricted to the characteristics that were public at the time is what a forecaster gains from knowing today which characteristics would later be published. The second is what the model does with a characteristic once it is public. If publication competes an edge away, a model refit each year should lean less on a characteristic after its paper appears.

7.1 Data and two decisions made before the models ran

read the committed outputs of 07_stage1_models.py and 08_stage1_eventtime.py

s1_r2_all = s1_r2[s1_r2["year"].astype(str) == "all"].set_index(["model", "set", "universe"])["r2"]

    return float(r["dm_t"].iloc[0])

# the target diagnostic that fixed the first decision

The panel is the United States part of the Jensen, Kelly, and Pedersen (2023) global factor data on WRDS: common stocks on the main exchanges, one primary security per firm, from 1963 to 2025. The target is next month’s excess return. The features are the 153 characteristics in that dataset for which a publication year is recorded, each ranked within its month across the whole universe and mapped to \([-1, 1]\), with missing values at zero. Two information sets are fitted on the same rows with the same grids and seeds. The public set holds the characteristics whose paper appeared before the test year, 21 of them in 1995; the full set holds all 153, which is the usual setup and contains look-ahead. The two sets coincide from 2021 on, so the gap between them is identified from the earlier test years. Test years run from 1995 to 2024; the forecasts made at the end of December 2024, which target January 2025, fall outside the window. Time is kept by the target month as in Section 6: training rows have target months before the validation block, the validation block is the eight years before the test year, and nothing is refit after validation, so the model scored on a test year is the one that was early-stopped or selected on the validation years.

Two decisions were made from diagnostics before any model was scored, and both changed the design.

The first concerns the target. The realised returns carry a few absurd values. In 12 of the 30 test years one stock-month holds more than half of the year’s total squared return, and the largest single share is 99.99 percent. A table of those rows by category, written before any model ran (output/stage1_target.csv), shows what they are: in 12 of the 12 dominated years the largest row has no CRSP return and no CRSP identifier, and in 11 of them the price is under ten cents. They are Compustat-sourced rows for securities CRSP does not cover. The remedy that follows is the one applied: the panel keeps only rows whose return comes from CRSP, which removes 2.5 percent of stock-months on average; the fitting and selection targets are clipped at the 0.1 and 99.9 percentiles of the training returns, except for the Huber regression, whose loss is its own protection; and every forecast is scored against the raw realised return. Because the tails sit in particular rows, the \(R^2\) is reported on three row sets: all 1,909,533 test rows, the rows outside the micro and nano size groups, and the rows whose realised return is inside \(\pm 100\) percent. A result that holds on one set and not another is reported as such.

The second concerns trading costs, and is described with the portfolios below.

7.2 Models

The models are those of Gu, Kelly, and Xiu (2020), in the same spirit of small grids: a Huber regression on all features, an elastic net, principal-component and partial-least-squares regressions, gradient boosted trees (Ke et al. 2017), and feed-forward networks with one, two and three hidden layers of 32, 16 and 8 units, each an average over five seeds. The trees are fitted twice, once with squared loss and once with a Huber loss, because the two disagree in a way the reader should see: the Huber-loss trees centre their forecasts below the realised mean, which gives them a negative \(R^2\) against a zero forecast and, at the same time, the highest rank correlation with realised returns of any model. Both are reported. Every setting tried is in output/stage1_tuning.csv, 540 rows.

7.3 Forecast accuracy

Four readings of Table 9 and Table 10.

The level is the one Gu, Kelly, and Xiu (2020) report for monthly stock returns. Against a zero forecast the full-information models explain between 0.22 and 0.55 percent of next month’s variation on all rows, the three-layer network highest at 0.55 percent and the Huber regression at 0.27.

The public set is below the full set in every cell of both tables. On all rows the gap is between 0.03 and 0.19 percentage points of \(R^2\); the Diebold-Mariano statistic of each model against its own public version is 1.5 for the Huber regression, 1.2 for the squared-loss trees and 2.1 for the three-layer network. Knowing in 1995 which characteristics would be published over the next twenty-five years is worth about 0.12 points of out-of-sample \(R^2\), and on rank correlation about 0.009. That is the size of the look-ahead in the usual setup, measured on the usual data.

The ordering of models is not stable across row sets. The squared-loss trees sit in the middle on all rows and near zero once returns beyond \(\pm 100\) percent are removed; the Huber-loss trees are negative on all rows, highest on that set, and highest on rank correlation on every set. A reader who wants one number should take the rank IC, which does not depend on where the tails fall: it is between 0.074 and 0.113 on all rows for the full set, and between 0.035 and 0.052 outside the micro and nano groups, with \(t\)-statistics above 4 throughout. The nonlinear models are not uniformly ahead of the linear ones on it.

Finally, 56 percent of the stock-months are micro or nano caps, and the forecasts are weaker outside them: the rank IC falls by about half and the Huber regression’s \(R^2\) on that set is 0.06 percent. The portfolios below make the same point in dollars.

7.4 Portfolios and the cost of trading them

Each month the stocks are sorted into deciles on the forecast, the top decile is held long and the bottom decile short, equal- or value-weighted, with and without the micro and nano groups. Turnover is half the sum of absolute weight changes, and each traded dollar is charged half a spread.

The second decision is which spread. The first pass charged half of the Corwin and Schultz (2012) estimate that comes with the panel, averaged over 21 days. The traded-weighted spread it implied in a value-weighted book was about one percent, which is too high after 2001 for stocks above the NYSE 20th size percentile, and the estimate is noisy and floored at zero, which pushes its mean up. The cost measure in this section is therefore the month’s mean closing quoted spread from the CRSP daily file, \((\text{ask} - \text{bid}) / \text{midpoint}\) on days with a positive quote, which Chung and Zhang (2014) show tracks TAQ effective spreads closely; for liquid stocks it is itself an upper bound, since trades print inside the quote. A quoted spread exists for 99.1 percent of the test stock-months (between 98.7 and 99.2 percent across the size groups) and prices at least 94 percent of traded weight in every book; the Corwin-Schultz estimate fills the gap. Corwin-Schultz is also reported as a bound: for every size group outside nano it is above the quoted spread, by a factor of about ten at the mega-cap median, so the net Sharpe ratio under it is a conservative reading for a value-weighted book. In the nano group it is below the quoted spread, so it is not a bound there. The Abdi and Ranaldo (2017) estimate from daily high, low and close is a third reading that needs no quotes.

Table 11 is why the choice matters. For mega and large caps the quoted spread median is 0.05 and 0.09 percent against Corwin-Schultz medians of 0.55 and 0.66; the two agree in the micro group and reverse in the nano group, where the quoted spread is wider. A value-weighted book puts 61 percent of its trading in mega caps, where the quoted spread charges it 0.24 percent and Corwin-Schultz would charge 0.70. The traded-weighted spreads sit above the panel medians within every group, as they should when the extreme deciles hold the less liquid stocks of each group and the spread distribution is skewed.

Three things in Table 12. Gross, the value-weighted books earn between 1.34 and 3.42 percent a month on the full set, the networks at the top. Net of costs the best is the network, 2 layers, full set, with an annualised Sharpe ratio of 1.09; the Huber regression nets 0.70. Under the Corwin-Schultz bound the same two books net 0.76 and 0.29, and several of the public-set linear books net nothing; the bound does not change the ordering.

The public set is below the full set in every book, gross and net. Whether the gap is more than noise is a question about the monthly difference between the two long-short returns, and Table 13 tests it two ways: the mean of the monthly difference in gross returns with a Newey-West \(t\)-statistic at twelve lags, and the difference in net Sharpe ratios with the Ledoit and Wolf (2008) test, which applies the delta method to the two means and two second moments under the same Newey-West covariance.

The gap survives the test for the linear models and not for the trees. For the value-weighted Huber book on all stocks the full set earns 0.47 percentage points a month more than the public set (t = 2.5), and its net Sharpe ratio is higher by 0.34 (Ledoit-Wolf t = 2.9), which is the difference between 0.70 and 0.36 in Table 12. The Sharpe difference clears t = 2 in all four books for Huber regression; elastic net; partial least squares; network, 1 layer; in none of the four for boosted trees, squared loss; boosted trees, Huber loss; and in some books for principal components; network, 2 layers; network, 3 layers. Over the 36 model-book pairs, 23 Sharpe differences and 23 mean differences clear t = 2. For the linear models, then, a backtest that uses every characteristic over the whole sample overstates the net Sharpe ratio that was available at the time by about a third of a unit, and the overstatement is not noise. For the trees the two sets are indistinguishable.

The equal-weighted books, in output/stage1_portfolio_summary.csv, are the ones that look spectacular and are not. Gross they earn Sharpe ratios of 1.1 to 3.4 on the full set, because they put between 61 and 82 percent of their trading in micro and nano caps. They pay 2.2 to 3.7 percent a month for it on the quoted spread and net between 0.09 and 0.77. The value-weighted books and the books without micro and nano caps are the ones an allocator could hold.

7.5 What the model uses, in event time around publication

For the full-information model the run saves, in every test year, the permutation importance of every characteristic: the rise in test mean squared error when that column is shuffled. Put in event time, \(e\) being the test year minus the characteristic’s publication year, the question is whether the model leans less on a characteristic once it is public:

\[ \mathrm{imp}_{c,y} \;=\; a_c + d_y + b\,\mathrm{post}_{c,y} + e_{c,y}, \qquad \mathrm{post}_{c,y} = \mathbf{1}[\,y \ge \text{pub}_c\,]. \]

Characteristic effects \(a_c\) absorb how useful a characteristic is on average, year effects \(d_y\) absorb anything that moves every importance in a year, and \(b\) is identified from the 132 characteristics whose publication year falls inside the test window. Importance enters in units of mean squared error scaled by \(10^4\) and as a share of the year’s total positive importance. A second specification replaces post with event-time bins, the five years before publication being the reference. Standard errors are clustered by characteristic and by year. The two-way covariance of Cameron, Gelbach, and Miller (2011) is not positive semi-definite in general, and here it was not: one bin coefficient came out with a negative variance. The matrix is made semi-definite by setting its negative eigenvalues to zero, as Cameron, Gelbach, and Miller (2011) suggest, and the standard errors reported are the ones after that step, which widens them.

Permutation importance in a linear model is about \(2\beta\,\mathrm{Cov}(y - \text{rest}, x)\) on the test rows. It rises when the model leans harder on the characteristic and when the characteristic still covaries with the return out of sample, and the two can be separated. The same design is run on two more outcomes saved beside the forecasts: the Huber regression’s slope on each characteristic, and the characteristic’s own monthly Spearman correlation with the realised return over the test year.

What the table shows, counted. There are 10 model-outcome pairs in the post specification and 40 binned coefficients. Of the post coefficients, 2 have |t| above 2, the Huber importance in error units, the Huber importance share; of the binned coefficients, 0 do. Every post coefficient on importance is positive, which is the opposite sign from the competed-away story, but only the Huber ones are distinguishable from zero, at t = 2.41 in error units and t = 2.01 as a share of the year’s total; the trees and the network sit at t = 1.04 and 1.14. With this many outcomes looked at, two coefficients near t = 2 are what a search of this size turns up on its own, and the paper does not claim more.

The decomposition rows say that, if there is a Huber effect, it sits in the model and not in the characteristic: the slope grows weakly after publication (\(\log|\beta|\) by 0.075, t = 0.81; \(|\beta|\) by 2.4 basis points, t = 1.65), and the characteristic’s own correlation with next month’s return does not move (+0.092 on the IC × 100, t = 0.37; -0.004 on its absolute value, t = -0.03). A published characteristic has, by construction, a long in-sample record in the training data, and an expanding-window regression weights it accordingly, which would produce this pattern without any change in the characteristic itself.

The post coefficient cannot yet be read as a publication effect, for two reasons. The earliest bin, six to ten years before publication, is below the reference for the Huber importance (t = -1.91), so the rise is already under way before the paper appears; working papers circulate for years before a journal issue, and the publication year in the characteristic list is a late date for the event. And publication is staggered, so this is a two-way fixed effects event study, and when the effect differs across publication cohorts the binned coefficients mix clean comparisons with ones that use already-published characteristics as controls (Goodman-Bacon 2021; Sun and Abraham 2021). The Sun and Abraham (2021) interaction-weighted version is the next step, and no claim about publication and model reliance is made until it is in.

7.6 What this section does and does not show

It shows, on the usual stock-level data, how much a forecaster gains from knowing in advance which characteristics would be published: a few tenths of a point of out-of-sample \(R^2\), a few hundredths of rank correlation, and a visible share of the Sharpe ratio of every book. For the linear models the gap in net Sharpe ratio survives a Ledoit-Wolf test in every book; for the trees it does not. It shows that the gross returns of the equal-weighted books are paid for in micro and nano caps, and that the quoted spread and the Corwin-Schultz bound give different answers on whether the public-set linear books survive costs. It does not show that publication changes what a model uses: two of ten post coefficients clear |t| = 2, both for the Huber importance, with a pre-trend in the same direction, and the cohort-robust version has not been run. It does not show which models are best: the ordering changes with the row set, and the Diebold-Mariano statistics among the full-set models are computed on the same squared loss whose sums the tails dominate. It does not measure decay in days, which is the next stage.

8 What the design cannot do, and what comes next

8.1 Calendar time and staggered treatment

Publication arrives at a different date for every signal, so Equation 1 is a two-way fixed effects regression with staggered adoption. Goodman-Bacon (2021) shows that such an estimator is a weighted average of all possible two-group comparisons, including comparisons that use already-published signals as controls for later-published ones. When the effect varies across signals or evolves over time, and decay that continues for years after publication is an effect that evolves, those comparisons enter with the wrong sign. Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) and Sun and Abraham (2021) estimate the effect using only not-yet-published signals as controls, and the same estimators absorb the calendar-time decline discussed in Section 4. This is the next thing to build, and it should change the number.

Regression discontinuity does not apply. It needs a running variable with a cutoff and units that cannot manipulate their position around it. Here the running variable would be calendar time, the cutoff is anticipated, since working papers circulate for years before a journal issue appears, and authors have some control over timing. Anticipation alone pushes part of the decay before the event and biases the estimate toward zero, so the post-publication decline measured here is a lower bound on the true one.

8.2 How fast, and to what floor

A three-window average says the edge fell. It does not say how quickly, or whether it fell to zero. The simple route fits

\[ \alpha_t \;=\; \phi + (\alpha_0 - \phi)\,e^{-\lambda t} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \text{half-life} \;=\; \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} \]

per signal, with \(\phi\) the floor. Grossman and Stiglitz (1980) says the floor should be positive, so estimating it tests that prediction. The better route is a state-space model,

\[ r_t = \alpha_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \alpha_t = \phi_i + \rho_i(\alpha_{t-1} - \phi_i) + \eta_t , \]

estimated by the Kalman filter and maximum likelihood (Durbin and Koopman 2012), which returns the floor and the half-life \(\ln 2 / (-\ln \rho_i)\) with standard errors from one estimation.

8.3 Who dies fast

The cross-section is where the arbitrage story becomes testable: decay should be faster where arbitrage is cheaper and where more capital has arrived. Illiquidity, market capitalisation, idiosyncratic volatility, short interest and institutional ownership are all computable from the CRSP panel built for Section 5. The Jensen, Kelly and Pedersen global factor data would turn the same hypothesis into a cross-country test, and Jacobs and Müller (2020) suggest what to expect.

8.4 Open items

  • Re-run on the McLean and Pontiff (2016) 97 to see whether the weaker channel separation is a composition effect.
  • Replace Equation 1 with the Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) and Sun and Abraham (2021) estimators and report how much the estimate moves; the same for the event-time regression on importance in Section 7.
  • Gross profitability as a third rebuilt signal; it needs Compustat and the CCM link.
  • Decay in days: the same public-against-full comparison on daily portfolio returns built from the CRSP daily file, which is the horizon a trading desk means by the word.
  • Sequence models on the stock-level panel, once the daily panel exists.

9 Reproducing this document

# The decay results need only the two free Chen and Zimmermann files in data/
quarto render paper/alpha-decay.qmd --to html

# The CRSP and forecasting sections read committed result files. To regenerate them:
python 03_crsp_pull.py          # WRDS subscription required
python 04_build_anomalies.py    # WRDS subscription required
python 05_ml_panel.py           # the two free files only, about ten minutes
python 06_jkp_pull.py           # the stock-level panel; WRDS subscription required
python 09_spreads.py            # closing quoted spreads from the CRSP daily file; WRDS
python 07_stage1_models.py --robust --crsp-only   # about a day on a laptop
python 08_stage1_eventtime.py   # the event-time tables and figures

# The version without the machine-learning section:
quarto render paper/alpha-decay.qmd --profile course
code 
# The three-window means recomputed here must match the ones 02_decay_panel.py wrote.
# If this assertion fires, the script and the paper have drifted apart.
saved = pd.read_csv(OUT / "result1_windows.csv", index_col=0)
assert saved.shape[0] == N_MATCHED, (saved.shape[0], N_MATCHED)
for c in ["in_sample", "post_sample", "post_pub"]:
    np.testing.assert_allclose(saved[c].mean(), table[c].mean(), rtol=1e-10)
print(f"verified against output/result1_windows.csv: "
      f"{N_MATCHED} signals, three windows match")
